title: Discounting: Pulling Future Money Back to the Present
subtitle: The reverse of compounding - the basis of every valuation
openingQuestion: Receiving 1 million after 5 years with a discount rate of 8%. What is the present value?
explanation: Discounting is the reverse calculation of compounding: instead of asking what an amount today will become, we ask how much a future amount is worth right now. Because the denominator carries an exponent, the farther out a cash flow is, the more heavily it gets compressed - at a 10% discount rate, an amount received twenty years out retains only about fifteen percent of its value. This is why the distant-future portion of a valuation model contributes far less than it feels like it should.

realWorldExample.company: Lottery winnings: lump sum or installments?
realWorldExample.description: When winning a large lottery, the winner is often given the choice of receiving everything at once (an already discounted lump sum) or receiving annual installments over 20-30 years (a larger nominal total) - a real-world application of discounting to compare the true value of the two options.

quiz.question: How does a cash flow further in the future (year 20 instead of year 5) compare in PV?
options: Higher, because it has more time to earn compound interest
Much lower, because it's divided by a far larger denominator
Equal, because the nominal amount hasn't changed at all
Exactly three times lower, matching the year gap
quiz.explanation: A year-20 cash flow is discounted 20 times: PV = FV / (1+r)^20. With r=10%, 1 million in year 20 is worth only 149,000 dong in PV today. This is why Terminal Value depends so heavily on the discount rate.

quiz.question: Why do two cash flows with the same total nominal amount (say, both 1 billion dong) but received at different times end up with different present values (PV)?
options: Because the risk of not receiving the money grows the longer you wait
Because inflation differs each year, so the amount loses value differently
Because each cash flow must be discounted separately, matched to its own timing
Because banks apply different fees for different receipt periods
quiz.explanation: This is why you can't directly compare cash flows at different times using their nominal totals - they must be converted to the same point in time (usually the present) via discounting before comparison, which is exactly what NPV and DCF do.

quiz.question: Receiving 500 million after 10 years, discount rate 8%. What is the approximate PV?
options: ≈ 250 million (= 500 ÷ 2, halved for ten years)
≈ 460 million (= 500 ÷ 1.08, discounting only one year)
≈ 1,079 million (= 500 × 1.08 to the 10th power, multiplying up)
≈ 232 million (= 500 ÷ 1.08 to the 10th power)
quiz.explanation: PV = 500 / 1.08^10 = 500 / 2.1589 ≈ 232 million. After ten years at an 8% discount rate, an amount retains less than half its value when converted back to today.

quiz.question: Why does Terminal Value in a DCF get scrutinized more closely than any other part of the model?
options: Because it makes up 60-80% of the value while being the hardest to forecast
Because it's the only part that doesn't need discounting to the present
Because valuation standards require it to be disclosed separately
Because it's always calculated using a multiple instead of cash flow
quiz.explanation: Most of the conclusion sits in the farthest-out cash flow, exactly where forecasting is weakest and the discount rate has the strongest effect. When reading a valuation, check Terminal Value's weight before debating anything else.

quiz.question: How are discounting and compounding related?
options: Two entirely different formulas mathematically
The same formula, running in opposite directions
Discounting uses simple interest, compounding uses compound interest
Compounding is for businesses, discounting is for individuals
quiz.explanation: Multiplying by (1+r)^n moves toward the future, dividing by (1+r)^n moves back to the present. Understanding one direction means understanding the other, and every DCF model is just that second direction repeated many times.

keyTakeaways: The farther out a cash flow → the smaller its PV → the more it depends on the discount rate

practicePrompt.question: Compounding calculates the future value of an amount of money today (FV = PV × (1+r)^n). What does discounting do in reverse, and why are these two calculations fundamentally a pair of inverses?
options: Discounting is compounding run backward: the same formula, moving from FV to PV
Discounting and compounding are two completely unrelated concepts in finance
Discounting only applies to bonds, while compounding only applies to savings deposits
Discounting always gives a larger result than compounding for the same amount and interest rate
practicePrompt.explanation: Discounting = compounding in reverse: PV = FV / (1+r)^n is exactly the reverse of FV = PV × (1+r)^n. Compounding answers 'how large will money today grow in the future', discounting answers 'how much is future money worth today' - the same relationship, viewed from two different directions in time.

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Try discounting in reverse
application.message: Take a future financial goal (e.g. 1 billion in 15 years), use PV = FV/(1+r)^n to calculate how much you need to have today or invest each year.
application.secondary: This is exactly how funds and banks value every financial asset.

sections.text: If compounding is the calculation that carries money from the present into the future, discounting is the reverse calculation: pulling a future amount back to its equivalent value today. This is exactly the foundational technique behind every discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation.

Compounding multiplies by (1+r)^n to move toward the future; discounting divides by (1+r)^n to move back to the present - the same formula, just used in the opposite direction. **Example:** 1,000,000 dong received after 20 years, discount rate 10%: PV = 1,000,000 / (1.1)^20 = 1,000,000 / 6.7275 ≈ 148,644 dong. Less than 15% of the original nominal value remains, since it's been discounted 20 times in a row.
Comparing cash flows at different points in time

You cannot directly compare two amounts received at two different times using their nominal figures. **Example:** 1 billion dong received today is clearly worth more than 1 billion dong received after 15 years, even though on paper it's the same amount. This is why a lump-sum lottery payment is always much smaller than the sum of all the annual installments combined - because the lump sum has already been discounted to its equivalent present value.

sections.label: Why Terminal Value gets scrutinized most
sections.text: In a 5-year DCF model, Terminal Value typically makes up 60-80% of total value - meaning most of the conclusion sits in the farthest-out cash flow, exactly where forecasting is weakest and r has the strongest effect. When reading a valuation, check Terminal Value's weight before debating anything else.

items: Discounting is the reverse operation of compounding, using the shared formula (1+r)^n
The further into the future a cash flow is, the more times it's discounted → the smaller its PV
Terminal Value in a DCF (very distant future cash flow) is extremely sensitive to the discount rate
To compare two cash flows at different points in time, you must always convert them to the same point in time first

lines: Every DCF model, from equity valuation to project appraisal, is just a chain of discounting calculations repeated many times.
